metadata.narrative: Our local water coalition is trying to understand Benton Harbor as a case study before we decide how to push our own city on aging water lines. Can you help me understand what actually went wrong there, why residents and advocates framed it as an environmental justice problem, and what changed after the petitioning and public pressure? What should we take away about bottled water, filters, corrosion control, pipe replacement, and government accountability if we want a practical advocacy plan rather than just a slogan?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Benton Harbor, Michigan, a four-square-mile city of about ten thousand people that is roughly eighty-five percent Black and nearly half living in poverty, first had lead detected in its drinking water in 2018 during routine testing by the state's environmental agency.

For at least three consecutive years the city's water tested above the federal lead action level of fifteen parts per billion, with some individual home samples reported as high as 469 to 605 parts per billion, levels rivaling or exceeding Flint at its worst.

The city had just emerged from six years under a state-appointed emergency financial manager when the lead levels were found, and regulators themselves described its Lake Michigan-fed water plant as "historically neglected" with a host of safety violations.

The underlying mechanism was the same one that caused Flint's crisis: aging lead service lines leach lead into water unless corrosion-control treatment is properly applied, and Benton Harbor's plant did not get corrosion control installed until March 2019, a full year after the danger was known.

Because the problem stemmed from corrosion of the pipes rather than a river source switch, it looked less dramatic than Flint from the outside, which advocates argued let officials treat it as a slow technical fix rather than an emergency.

Residents and organizers, led by the Rev. Edward Pinkney and the volunteer Benton Harbor Community Water Council, framed the crisis explicitly as environmental and racial injustice, pointing out that the mostly white neighboring city of St. Joseph, separated only by a river, has a poverty rate of about six percent versus Benton Harbor's forty-three percent and never developed the same lead problem.

They also compared the state's inaction to the EPA's swift 2021 Emergency Administrative Order for majority-white Clarksburg, West Virginia, arguing Benton Harbor's contamination was as severe or worse yet drew a much slower response, a disparity Michigan's own Environmental Justice Public Advocate office later contextualized using federal EJScreen data showing the city in the ninety-fifth percentile for cumulative environmental-justice burden.

While officials deliberated, the Community Water Council itself organized bottled-water drives and resident education for years before any government agency stepped in, with one resident recalling, "we can't keep standing in line for water, we have rights."
Internal agency records later obtained by reporters showed that advocates' repeated emails and a formal EPA petition were what actually forced faster action, not routine oversight.

On September 9, 2021, twenty environmental and civil-rights groups, including the Great Lakes Environmental Law Center and the NRDC, filed a formal EPA petition demanding emergency intervention and full lead-line replacement.

The day before that petition was filed, Governor Whitmer announced twenty million dollars for Benton Harbor and two hundred million statewide to remove lead lines within five years, a timeline residents rejected as too slow.

In October 2021 the state advised residents to stop drinking or cooking with tap water entirely, and in November the EPA issued an emergency order requiring the city to notify residents promptly of lead exceedances, improve chlorine disinfection and orthophosphate corrosion control, tighten disinfectant-byproduct monitoring, repair treatment-plant filters, and bring in an independent evaluator.

Local officials separately declared their own state of emergency to draw federal attention, and by late October Whitmer signed a directive compressing the replacement timeline from five years to eighteen months, backed initially by $18.6 million in combined state and EPA grant funding.

The practical result for your coalition is that corrosion control alone is not a solution but a stabilizer: Michigan officials reported lead levels falling toward compliance after treatment adjustments, yet state advocates insisted bottled water continue "until lead service line replacement is finished," because even compliant levels still carry risk.

Filters followed a similar arc worth learning from: certified lead-reducing filters were distributed in 2019, officials later paused endorsing them pending a study, and an EPA-led test of nearly two hundred homes in 2022 found that properly used filters reduced lead to within federal guidelines in almost every case, but many households were not shown how to install or maintain them correctly.

That finding argues for pairing any filter distribution with hands-on installation training and cartridge-replacement reminders, not just handing out hardware, since experts noted trust in filters was easily undermined even when the devices worked.

Bottled water proved essential as an immediate stopgap but became its own burden, with roughly ten thousand residents relying on daily distribution sites, long lines, and delivery requests for homebound residents, and one water researcher observed that "once communities get on to bottled water, it is a habit, and it is hard to get off."

Pipe replacement itself moved fast once political will existed: by October 2022 the state reported ninety-eight percent of roughly 4,400 identified lead lines replaced, with full completion targeted for spring 2023, a pace regulators called far faster than the federal law's default thirty-three-year allowance and swifter per-pipe than Newark's comparable project.

On accountability, the record is mixed and instructive: no state or local official admitted responsibility even as funding flowed, Michigan's environmental agency defended itself by pointing to actions it says exceeded minimum legal requirements, and the EPA's own inspector general opened an investigation into whether the federal response itself was too slow.

Families also turned to the courts, with a federal lawsuit filed on behalf of roughly four hundred exposed children explicitly invoking Flint's six-hundred-million-dollar settlement as the accountability benchmark government and contractors should meet.

For your advocacy plan, the Benton Harbor case suggests documenting exceedance data publicly and repeatedly rather than trusting quiet compliance timelines, building a coalition that pairs grassroots groups with national legal organizations to file a formal emergency petition once a real deadline is needed, demanding corrosion-control fixes and certified filters and bottled water simultaneously rather than sequentially, insisting on plain-language installation education wherever filters are distributed, pushing for a compressed, publicly tracked pipe-replacement schedule instead of accepting multi-year regulatory defaults, and treating litigation and inspector-general oversight as necessary companions to executive promises, since funding announcements alone did not equal admitted responsibility in Benton Harbor.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

answer.text: Benton Harbor, Michigan, a four-square-mile city of about ten thousand people that is roughly eighty-five percent Black and nearly half living in poverty, first had lead detected in its drinking water in 2018 during routine testing by the state's environmental agency.

For at least three consecutive years the city's water tested above the federal lead action level of fifteen parts per billion, with some individual home samples reported as high as 469 to 605 parts per billion, levels rivaling or exceeding Flint at its worst.

The city had just emerged from six years under a state-appointed emergency financial manager when the lead levels were found, and regulators themselves described its Lake Michigan-fed water plant as "historically neglected" with a host of safety violations.

The underlying mechanism was the same one that caused Flint's crisis: aging lead service lines leach lead into water unless corrosion-control treatment is properly applied, and Benton Harbor's plant did not get corrosion control installed until March 2019, a full year after the danger was known.

Because the problem stemmed from corrosion of the pipes rather than a river source switch, it looked less dramatic than Flint from the outside, which advocates argued let officials treat it as a slow technical fix rather than an emergency.

Residents and organizers, led by the Rev. Edward Pinkney and the volunteer Benton Harbor Community Water Council, framed the crisis explicitly as environmental and racial injustice, pointing out that the mostly white neighboring city of St. Joseph, separated only by a river, has a poverty rate of about six percent versus Benton Harbor's forty-three percent and never developed the same lead problem.

They also compared the state's inaction to the EPA's swift 2021 Emergency Administrative Order for majority-white Clarksburg, West Virginia, arguing Benton Harbor's contamination was as severe or worse yet drew a much slower response, a disparity Michigan's own Environmental Justice Public Advocate office later contextualized using federal EJScreen data showing the city in the ninety-fifth percentile for cumulative environmental-justice burden.

While officials deliberated, the Community Water Council itself organized bottled-water drives and resident education for years before any government agency stepped in, with one resident recalling, "we can't keep standing in line for water, we have rights."
Internal agency records later obtained by reporters showed that advocates' repeated emails and a formal EPA petition were what actually forced faster action, not routine oversight.

On September 9, 2021, twenty environmental and civil-rights groups, including the Great Lakes Environmental Law Center and the NRDC, filed a formal EPA petition demanding emergency intervention and full lead-line replacement.

The day before that petition was filed, Governor Whitmer announced twenty million dollars for Benton Harbor and two hundred million statewide to remove lead lines within five years, a timeline residents rejected as too slow.

In October 2021 the state advised residents to stop drinking or cooking with tap water entirely, and in November the EPA issued an emergency order requiring the city to notify residents promptly of lead exceedances, improve chlorine disinfection and orthophosphate corrosion control, tighten disinfectant-byproduct monitoring, repair treatment-plant filters, and bring in an independent evaluator.

Local officials separately declared their own state of emergency to draw federal attention, and by late October Whitmer signed a directive compressing the replacement timeline from five years to eighteen months, backed initially by $18.6 million in combined state and EPA grant funding.

The practical result for your coalition is that corrosion control alone is not a solution but a stabilizer: Michigan officials reported lead levels falling toward compliance after treatment adjustments, yet state advocates insisted bottled water continue "until lead service line replacement is finished," because even compliant levels still carry risk.

Filters followed a similar arc worth learning from: certified lead-reducing filters were distributed in 2019, officials later paused endorsing them pending a study, and an EPA-led test of nearly two hundred homes in 2022 found that properly used filters reduced lead to within federal guidelines in almost every case, but many households were not shown how to install or maintain them correctly.

That finding argues for pairing any filter distribution with hands-on installation training and cartridge-replacement reminders, not just handing out hardware, since experts noted trust in filters was easily undermined even when the devices worked.

Bottled water proved essential as an immediate stopgap but became its own burden, with roughly ten thousand residents relying on daily distribution sites, long lines, and delivery requests for homebound residents, and one water researcher observed that "once communities get on to bottled water, it is a habit, and it is hard to get off."

Pipe replacement itself moved fast once political will existed: by October 2022 the state reported ninety-eight percent of roughly 4,400 identified lead lines replaced, with full completion targeted for spring 2023, a pace regulators called far faster than the federal law's default thirty-three-year allowance and swifter per-pipe than Newark's comparable project.

On accountability, the record is mixed and instructive: no state or local official admitted responsibility even as funding flowed, Michigan's environmental agency defended itself by pointing to actions it says exceeded minimum legal requirements, and the EPA's own inspector general opened an investigation into whether the federal response itself was too slow.

Families also turned to the courts, with a federal lawsuit filed on behalf of roughly four hundred exposed children explicitly invoking Flint's six-hundred-million-dollar settlement as the accountability benchmark government and contractors should meet.
